clue.text: Footwork by footballer brings strong reaction

parts.note: a kick is a piece of footwork
a back is a defending footballer, placed next to the first piece

explanation.surface: A footballer's fancy footwork draws a big response from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' here means placed beside, so the footballer follows the footwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A kickback is a sharp recoil or violent response, as when a gun or engine jerks back.

clue.text: Communist sustaining friendly relations

indicators.note: in a down clue, sustaining means holding up from underneath, so one piece is placed below the other

parts.note: kind means friendly and warm
red is the traditional label for a communist

explanation.surface: A communist keeping up good relations with others.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindred means one's family, people related by blood, so it is a plural noun for relations.

clue.text: Look out when a youth carrying a note boards a train

parts.note: cave, Latin for beware, was schoolboy slang for look out; the last letter waits

indicators.note: carrying means holding something inside
to board is to get on and go inside

parts.note: a lad is a youth; the note sits between the two pieces
C is a note of the musical scale
the end of the warning word, closing round the rest

explanation.surface: Watch out as a young man with a banknote gets on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: Cave, Latin for beware, was the lookout's cry in British public schools. 'train' is not a railway train but a long procession.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavalcade is a procession of riders or vehicles, and a train can mean a long line of followers.

clue.text: Black root for sprout

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
to root for a side is to urge it on

explanation.surface: A black root grown to make a sprout, as if gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'root for' looks like gardening but means cheer on, a sense from American sport.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to begin growing or put out buds, which is what a plant does when it sprouts.

clue.text: Made firm reduce order that's turned up

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from the bottom upwards
to reduce something is to make it shorter, so a letter goes

parts.note: a decree is an official order

explanation.surface: Instructions to make something firm and to reduce an order that has been reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made firm' reads as one phrase meaning hardened, but 'Made' alone is the definition, in the sense of forced to act.
explanation.definitionFit: Coerced means forced by pressure, and to be made to do something is to be compelled.

clue.text: Knowing about one series of books — Hardy perhaps?

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word is wrapped around the others

parts.note: fly is slang for knowing or shrewd
the Roman numeral for one
the New Testament is a series of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy, author of a series of novels, is a knowing writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H disguises 'hardy' as the novelist; the question mark flags that the definition works by a pun on hard-y.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as hard-y, the definition hints at something hard like flint; flinty means stony, harsh and unyielding.

clue.text: Anticipation is a help to a marksman

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ability to see what will happen
second meaning: split as ..., the front aiming sight on a gun barrel

explanation.surface: Being able to anticipate a target's movement helps a sharpshooter.
explanation.walkthrough: The fore sight is the sight near the muzzle of a rifle, lined up with the rear sight to aim.
explanation.definitionFit: Foresight means looking ahead and planning for the future, which is anticipation; it is also the gun's front sight.

clue.text: Jewish kings go up in number

definitions.note: loose: Israeli means of Israel, not Jewish

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside another
in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the first half of II, the Roman numeral two
King Lear is Shakespeare's king, so Lears are kings
the second half of II, closing round the rest

explanation.surface: Jewish kings rise in number.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is II, two in Roman numerals, holding the reversed kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel is the Jewish state, so its citizens and things are loosely described with this adjective.

clue.text: Feature about bridge players passing

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: a trait is a feature; its last letters close round
North and South are partners at the bridge table
the rest of the word for a feature

explanation.surface: A newspaper feature about bridge players who pass in the bidding.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAIT goes round NS.
explanation.definitionFit: Transit is the act of passing through or across a place, so the noun matches passing.

clue.text: A way of shopping in the Australian outback

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for hire purchase, buying on credit
second meaning: the remote, empty interior of Australia

explanation.surface: Someone goes shopping somewhere in the remote Australian bush.
explanation.walkthrough: Hire purchase means paying for goods in instalments, and the British nickname for it suggests you never finish paying.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial name both for paying by instalments and for the uninhabited Australian desert regions.

clue.text: In Yorkshire, a morning paper

indicators.note: In says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: spanning the end of the county name, the article and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone in Yorkshire buys a morning newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a morning paper' reads as a newspaper, but paper alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ream is a standard bundle of paper sheets, usually five hundred, so the word names a quantity of paper.

clue.text: Rides in a boat within the Canaries

indicators.note: within puts one thing inside another

parts.note: rollers are a breed of singing canary
a coaster is a small ship trading along the coast

explanation.surface: A boat trip around the Canary Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Canaries' looks like the islands off Africa, but means the birds: rollers are a singing breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Roller-coasters are fairground rides, so they are an example of what the definition describes.

clue.text: Exhausted doctor, first class chap

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for doctor
A1 means first class, with the 1 as the letter I
Ned is a man's name, a stand-in for any chap

explanation.surface: A worn-out doctor who is otherwise a first-rate fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, top quality, is written AI in crosswords because the digit 1 looks like the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Drained and exhausted both describe someone with all their energy used up, as synonyms.

clue.text: Tom's friend, for instance, accepting Reginald's present

parts.note: Harry East is Tom's friend in Tom Brown's Schooldays

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: e.g. means for instance
Reg is the short form of Reginald

explanation.surface: A friend of Tom's, for example, takes a gift from Reginald.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown's Schooldays is a Victorian novel about Rugby School, in which Harry East is Tom's best friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A chocolate egg given at Easter is a gift, so the answer is an example of a present.

clue.text: Selfish people say it's so wrong

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are out of their proper places and must be rearranged

parts.note: e.g. means for example, as 'say' can
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Somebody complains that selfish people claim something is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like a verb of speaking but stands for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: Egoists put their own interests first, so they are self-centred people, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Messy site reorganized and put in order

indicators.note: reorganized means arranged again in a new way

parts.note: all the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A messy site has been tidied up and organised.
explanation.definitionFit: To systemise is to arrange according to a system, which is putting things into an orderly arrangement.

clue.text: Be economical, in vain

wordplay.note: the instruction a thrifty person follows, read as two words: consume a smaller amount

explanation.surface: An attempt to save money proves futile.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as USE LESS, the answer is an instruction to be thrifty.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in vain achieves nothing, and an effort that achieves nothing is futile or ineffective.

clue.text: An unidentified person, "Anon", embraced me with energy

indicators.note: embraced means held in the arms, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon
taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy, added at the end

explanation.surface: An anonymous stranger hugged me enthusiastically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anon' looks like the short form of anonymous, matching the definition, but here it is the archaic adverb meaning shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone means some person not named or known, the same as an unidentified individual.

clue.text: Grease coating some rope

indicators.note: coating means covering on all sides, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: lard is grease; its last letters close round
any can mean some, as in have you any?
the rest of the word for grease

explanation.surface: Grease is smeared over a length of rope.
explanation.walkthrough: LARD goes round ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: A lanyard is a short rope or cord, used on ships for securing things or worn round the neck.

clue.text: Walks over one not strictly 1 dn

parts.note: steps are paces taken when walking
on can mean over, as in a lid on a box

explanation.surface: Someone walks over a person who is not quite a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is KINDRED, blood relations: a stepson is family by marriage, not by blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepson is a spouse's son from an earlier union, so he is related only by marriage.

clue.text: Sink for keeping coal in

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to sink a ship deliberately by holing it
second meaning: a metal bucket kept by the fireplace for coal

explanation.surface: A kitchen sink used for storing coal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like a kitchen basin, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To scuttle a ship is to sink it on purpose; a coal scuttle is the container for fuel.

clue.text: Edward I provided soaring church building

parts.note: Ed is short for Edward
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, soaring means rising, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: if means provided that
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: King Edward I funded a lofty church building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edward I' reads as the king, but splits into a name and a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice is a large, imposing building, so the two nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: Flowers, say, gone astray

indicators.note: astray means gone wrong, out of their proper places

parts.note: all the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Some flowers have gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like an aside meaning for example, but its letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small posy or bunch of sweet-smelling blooms.

clue.text: Use my skin and bones to make mischief

indicators.note: to make says these words are the raw material to be worked into something new

parts.note: every letter of these words except the joining word

explanation.surface: A grisly threat: someone will use your skin and bones for some prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the fodder words and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey business is an idiom for playful trickery or underhand dealing, which is mischief.

clue.text: Part of the British Isles a part of America? …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small island of the Inner Hebrides, off western Scotland
second meaning: a place name used in the United States, for towns and a New York college

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the American sense is loose: several small US towns share the island's name. The trailing dots link this clue to the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is the Scottish island where St Columba founded his monastery, and the same name labels several American places.

clue.text: … and another part once where new GIs trained

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: all the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A former British region where newly arrived American soldiers did their training.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition carries on from 22: another part of the British Isles, but only once, since this division of Yorkshire was abolished in 1974. 'trained' looks like a verb, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Riding was one of the three historic administrative divisions of Yorkshire, now no longer a county.

clue.text: Salt water to follow

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: Salt water comes after something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt water' reads as one phrase, but 'Salt' alone is the definition: an old salt is a veteran sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both salt and sea-dog are informal names for an experienced old sailor.

clue.text: Badly cut, see!

parts.note: to sever is to cut through
a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely in Cambridgeshire is one

explanation.surface: Someone shows off a nasty gash: look, I'm badly cut!
explanation.walkthrough: 'see!' looks like an exclamation, but a see is a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Badly and severely both mean seriously or harshly, as in hurt badly; the two adverbs are synonyms.
